Neither. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results, so five versus ten is the wrong question.

Here's an everyday version. Say you're planning a group project, and splitting it among 10 people means 10 people to brief, 10 pieces to merge and 10 chances for someone to misread the plan. If the pieces really are independent, like 10 people each researching a different company, more people helps. If the pieces depend on each other, the coordination costs more than the extra hands save.

Agents work the same way. Anthropic's write-up of its multi-agent research system gives the numbers:
- A single agent uses about 4× the tokens of a chat.
- A multi-agent system uses about 15× the tokens of a chat.
- That gain paid off for broad research with many independent directions. The post says it fits poorly when agents must share the same context or depend heavily on each other.

Your assistant looks like the poor fit. Answering from a manual, checking the calendar and booking all hang off one student's request, and a booking needs the answer and the calendar result together. With a small budget, 15× is a heavy price.

So start with the smallest design that works: one agent with three tools (manual search, calendar check, booking). Fixed steps, like confirming a booking, can be plain workflow code. Add a second agent only when you can name a specific job that is independent and large, for example one that would flood the main context with manual text.

That's also your design-review defense: "we added an agent only where a measured problem justified its cost."

Quick check: if you split into a "manuals agent" and a "booking agent", what would they have to pass back and forth to handle "Can I use the laser cutter Friday, and how do I load the material?"

Source: [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

I can turn this into a short lesson on workflows versus agents versus multi-agent systems if you'd like.
